mcqs.question: Why does the composite validator collect violations from every rule instead of stopping at the first failure?
options: Because rules are guaranteed to run in a random order otherwise
So the caller receives every problem with the object in a single pass, which is what makes the rules genuinely composable and useful for something like a form UI
Because ValidationRule<T> requires exactly one violation per check() call
It doesn't matter — stopping early and collecting everything produce the same result
mcqs.explanation: Aggregating every rule's output in one pass is exactly what a form needs to show a user all their mistakes at once, and it's what makes rules independently composable. Rule order isn't randomized by this design, check() can return any number of violations including zero, and stopping early gives a materially worse result.

mcqs.question: Why couldn't DateRangeRule be expressed if ValidationRule<T> only passed a single field's value instead of the whole target object?
options: Because a language rule prevents a check from referencing more than one variable
Because comparing two dates always requires a separate comparator class
The rule needs both startDate and endDate from the same object at once, which a single-field interface has no way to provide
Because cross-field rules must always be written as exceptions, not as ValidationRule<T> implementations
mcqs.explanation: A cross-field check inherently needs more than one field's data simultaneously, so the interface must hand over the whole object rather than one value. There's no such variable-reference restriction, date comparison needs no special comparator, and this rule is exactly a ValidationRule<T>, not an exception.

mcqs.question: How does the design handle a rule that needs to check more than one field on an object, like start and end dates?
options: It requires a separate CrossFieldRule interface distinct from ValidationRule<T>
It's not supported — cross-field checks have to happen outside the validation framework
It requires the object to expose its fields as a single combined string first
No special handling is needed — since Rule<T> already receives the whole target object, a cross-field rule is implemented as an ordinary ValidationRule<T>
mcqs.explanation: Because the interface is designed around the whole object rather than a single field, a cross-field rule needs no special type — it's the same ValidationRule<T> every other rule implements. There's no separate interface, no exclusion from the framework, and no string-combining step involved.

mcqs.question: Why is validating inside the domain object's own constructor a weaker design than a separate set of ValidationRule<T> objects?
options: It couples validation to construction, so you can't reuse the same rules for a partial update, can't collect all violations across a batch, and can't add or remove a rule without touching the domain class
Constructors are not allowed to throw exceptions in most languages
It makes the object immutable, which the validation framework requires it not to be
It's actually the recommended design, since it keeps validation closest to the data
mcqs.explanation: Baking validation into a constructor ties every use of that data to one throw-on-first behavior, blocking reuse, batch aggregation, and independent rule composition. Constructors can throw fine in most languages, immutability is unrelated, and this coupling is the actual weakness, not a recommended pattern.
